title: Day, night and the seasons
keyIdea: In the day the sky is light and we see the sun. At night it is dark and we see the moon and stars. The sun comes up in the morning, is high at midday and goes down in the evening. A year has four seasons that go round in order: winter, spring, summer and autumn. Winter is cold and summer is warm.

kid: In the day it is light. The sun is in the sky. At night it is dark. We see the moon and the stars.
The sun comes up in the morning. It is low in the sky. At midday it is up high. In the evening it goes down. Then it is night.
The sun does not go to bed. At night it shines on kids on the other side of the world. In the morning we see it come up again.
A year has four seasons. Winter is cold. In spring, flowers grow. Summer is warm. In autumn, leaves fall off the trees. Then it is winter again.
adult: This is early science about the world around us. The EYFS early learning goal The Natural World asks children to understand some important changes in the natural world, including the seasons. Development Matters asks Reception children to notice the effect of changing seasons. Year 1 of the English national curriculum covers seasonal changes. Children observe changes across the four seasons, describe the weather for each, and notice how day length varies. In the US, NGSS 1-ESS1-1 covers the patterns of the sun, moon and stars. 1-ESS1-2 links the amount of daylight to the time of year.

Key words for this age: day, night, light, dark, sunrise, sunset, morning, afternoon, evening, weather, and the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter). The sun seems to move across the sky because the Earth spins once a day. Children meet that model in Year 5 (Earth and space), so for now we say the sun comes up and goes down. In the UK, winter is roughly December to February and summer is June to August. Summer days are long and light; winter days are short.

Common mistakes: thinking the sun goes to sleep or goes away at night (it is daytime on the other side of the world). Thinking the moon only comes out at night (it is often in the day sky too). Thinking there are no stars in the day (the bright sky hides them). And thinking summer comes straight after winter. Be careful with seasons talk if your family has lived elsewhere. In Australia December is summer, and near the equator many places have a wet season and a dry season instead.

In the lab your child sorts the sun, moon, stars and a rainbow into the day sky or the night sky. They drag the sun from morning to midday to evening until night falls, and put the parts of their own day in order. Then they go round the seasons wheel and match weather and clothes to each season. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Look out of the same window at breakfast, after lunch and at bedtime, and ask 'Where is the sun now?' On a clear evening, look for the moon and the first star together. Once a season, take a photo of the same tree and put the photos in order.

practice.prompt: Day and night: what can you see in the sky at night?
practice.hint: Night is dark. What shines in the dark sky?
practice.explain: At night we see the moon and the stars. The sun is shining on the other side of the world.

practice.prompt: The sun comes up once every morning. How many times does it come up in {n} days?
practice.hint: Each day has one morning, and the sun comes up once each morning. Count the days.
practice.explain: One sunrise each day, so {n} days have {n} sunrises.

practice.hint: Think of the seasons wheel: winter, then the season when flowers start to grow.
practice.explain: After winter comes spring. Then summer, then autumn, then winter again.

practice.prompt: You see {n} stars in the night sky. A cloud covers 1 of them. How many stars can you still see?
practice.hint: The cloud hides just 1 star. Take 1 away from {n}.
practice.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. The hidden star is still there, behind the cloud.

pool.prompt: Where is the sun at midday?
pool.hint: In the lab, you dragged the sun up. Where was it in the middle of the day?
pool.explain: At midday the sun is high in the sky. In the morning and evening it is low.

pool.prompt: Where does the sun go at night?
choices: It shines on the other side of the world
It goes to sleep in bed
pool.hint: The sun is not alive, so it cannot sleep. Is it still shining somewhere?
pool.explain: The sun keeps shining. At night it is day for children on the other side of the world.

pool.prompt: Which season is cold, with frost and sometimes snow?
pool.hint: Which season do we wear a woolly hat and gloves?
pool.explain: Winter is the cold season. Summer is warm, and spring gets warmer.

pool.prompt: Leaves turn brown and fall off the trees. Which season is it?
pool.hint: This season comes after summer and before winter.
pool.explain: In autumn the leaves fall. In spring new leaves and flowers grow.

pool.prompt: What do you do in the morning?
pool.hint: Morning is the start of the day, when the sun comes up.
pool.explain: In the morning we wake up and eat breakfast. Pyjamas and bed are for night.

pool.prompt: Can you ever see the moon in the day?
pool.hint: Look up on a clear afternoon. Is there a pale moon?
pool.explain: Yes. We see the moon best at night, but it is often in the day sky too.

pool.prompt: It is night. You count {n} stars. Then 2 more stars come out. How many stars can you see now?
pool.hint: Start at {n} and count on 2 more stars.
pool.explain: {n} and 2 more make {=n+2}. More stars show as the sky gets darker.

pool.prompt: Which comes first in the day?
pool.hint: The sun comes up at the start of the day. What is that part called?
pool.explain: Morning comes first, then afternoon and evening, then night.

pool.prompt: Why can't we see the stars in the day?
choices: Stars are only made at night
pool.hint: The stars are still there. What makes the day sky so bright?
pool.explain: The stars are always there. In the day the sun is so bright that we cannot see them.

pool.prompt: {n} children play in the park in the afternoon. In the evening, 1 more child comes to watch the sunset. How many children are there now?
pool.hint: Start at {n}, then count on 1 more child.
pool.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}. Sunset is in the evening, when the sun goes down.
